diapos.titre: How to work in this course
points: Programming starts from **zero**: no prior knowledge of computing is needed
About **3 hours** of personal work a week, done regularly
**Test yourself** instead of rereading; **space out** your revision
Work on each tutorial exercise **before** opening the solution
Learn each term in **French** and in **English**
diapos.notes: Open the “How to learn this course” page and show the “A typical week” table: five moments, three hours in all. Stress this point: a review of research on the psychology of learning (Dunlosky et al., 2013) ranks testing yourself and spacing out revision among the most useful techniques; rereading and highlighting give a feeling of mastery, but little of it stays. Reassure students about Python: we start from zero.

consignes: Have you ever used a chatbot?
Do you have a laptop? An Internet connection at home?
In which language do you prefer to read technical documentation?
What do you expect from this course?
diapos.materiel: The printed questionnaire, one sheet per student
diapos.notes: 10 min. Collect the sheets without commenting on the answers in public. The answers about equipment will help you form the pairs for the lab sessions (TP): put each student who has no computer with a student who has one. The preferred reading language will tell you which students to point toward the English or Arabic version of the site.

consignes: For each object, vote by a show of hands: AI or not AI?
Calculator · spellchecker · spam filter · machine translator
Spot the objects that divide the class
A volunteer from each side justifies their vote in one sentence
diapos.notes: 15 min. Count the votes and write the results on the board; keep them for the end of the teacher input. Give no answers: the aim is to bring disagreements to light. Conclusion to draw: if we disagree, we first need to define what we call “artificial intelligence”.
20 min of teacher input, based on the lesson “What is artificial intelligence?” in chapter 1. Announce that you will then come back to the eight objects the class voted on.

diapos.legende: The Dartmouth workshop: the term “artificial intelligence” becomes the name of a research field
diapos.source: Proposal written in 1955 by McCarthy, Minsky, Rochester and Shannon
diapos.notes: Tell the story: in 1955, John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester and Claude Shannon asked for funding to bring researchers together at Dartmouth College, in the United States, in the summer of 1956. Their hypothesis: every aspect of learning and intelligence could be described precisely enough for a machine to simulate it. This workshop is considered the birth of the field. Add straight away that there is no single definition: there is no agreement on what the word “intelligence” itself means.

diapos.definition: A system that perceives its environment and acts on it to achieve a goal.
diapos.exemple: A spam filter “perceives” the text of an email and “acts” by putting it in the right folder.
diapos.notes: This is how the standard textbook by Stuart Russell and Peter Norvig, *Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach* (1995), presents AI: as the study of agents. Ask for another agent among the eight objects voted on. Possible answers: the GPS perceives a position and suggests a route; the thermostat perceives the temperature and acts on the heating. Point out that this definition is very broad: it is not enough to settle the question.

diapos.definition: The set of computing methods that allow a machine to perform tasks we usually associate with human intelligence: recognizing, classifying, predicting, reasoning, planning, understanding or producing language.
diapos.exemple: Recognizing the characters of an old newspaper (OCR), translating between Arabic and French, sorting emails.
diapos.notes: This is the course’s working definition. Stress that it is about observable tasks: it says nothing about what the machine “understands”. Add that talking about “AI” in the singular is misleading: it is a family of techniques (rules written by experts, exploring possibilities, learning from examples, neural networks). Have students write down the question to ask about any result produced by “an AI”: which technique, trained on which data, for which task?

diapos.titre: Why AI matters for literary studies

points: An Italian Jesuit indexes the works of Thomas Aquinas, with help from IBM
Often given as the origin of the **digital humanities** (*humanités numériques*)
No one can read every novel published in the 19th century
**Distant reading** (*lecture distante*): thousands of texts, measurable features
It does not replace close reading

diapos.notes: For a comparatist, Moretti is the reference: “Conjectures on World Literature” (2000), then *Distant Reading* (2013). Measurable features: genres, titles, character networks, the movement of forms from one language to another. Two concrete uses from chapter 1: in 2019, Florian Cafiero and Jean-Baptiste Camps provided quantitative arguments in favor of Molière in the controversy that set him against Corneille; you can also align a novel by Naguib Mahfouz sentence by sentence with its French and English translations, to compare the translators’ choices.

points: Spam filter: an agent that sorts emails
Machine translator: a narrow AI
Search engine: AI in everyday life
GPS: searching for a route among possibilities
Chatbot: a large language model
Calculator: is calculating an “intelligent” task?
Thermostat: it perceives and acts; is that enough?
Spellchecker: a dictionary, or a learned model?

diapos.notes: Go back to the votes on the board. For each object, ask the question of the definition: does it perform a task associated with human intelligence (recognizing, classifying, predicting, planning, producing language)? The first five are examples from chapter 1, where planning a route between Médéa and Algiers illustrates “state-space search”. For the other three, accept both answers if they are justified by the technique assumed: what counts is the justification, not the verdict.
25 min in all: the short version of the activity in the guide, with two witnesses, five minutes of questions, a vote and a discussion.

diapos.texte: I propose to consider the question, “Can machines think?”
diapos.source: Alan M. Turing, “Computing Machinery and Intelligence”, *Mind*, 1950
diapos.notes: This is the first sentence of the article, quoted here in Turing’s own words (the French slides give the course’s translation). Explain Turing’s move: rather than defining “thinking”, he proposes an observable test. In his original game, an interrogator must guess in writing who is the man and who is the woman; then a machine takes one of the places. If the interrogator cannot tell the machine from the human, the machine is behaving intelligently: this is the “Turing test”.

diapos.titre: Let’s play: which one is the machine?
consignes: Two witnesses, out of sight: X answers sincerely, Y plays the machine
The class asks its questions in writing, on strips of paper
Five minutes of questions per witness; the teacher reads the answers aloud
Show of hands: which one is the machine? Then the reveal
Discussion: what gave the machine away?
diapos.materiel: Strips of paper, a place out of sight, the rule card given to Y
diapos.notes: Timing: roles 3 min, questions 10 min (five minutes per witness, the length of time Turing mentions), vote 5 min, discussion for the rest. Discreetly give Y the rule card from the next slide, which you will only project after the vote. Read all the answers yourself: handwriting would give the witnesses away. Variation: Y is a chatbot whose answers you read out; the question then becomes “what does deceiving prove?”.

points: The question contains “you” → “Why are you asking me that question?”
It contains a word about family → “Tell me about your family.”
It asks for a calculation → wait thirty seconds, then answer
Otherwise → “I am not sure I understand. Could you rephrase that?”
diapos.notes: Project it only after the vote. These rules are in the spirit of ELIZA, the program by Joseph Weizenbaum (MIT, 1966) that imitated a psychotherapist by rephrasing the user’s sentences. Ask: what gave the machine away? Should it imitate our mistakes? In Turing’s example, the machine answers an addition after about thirty seconds, and gets it wrong.

diapos.question: Is deceiving the interrogator the same as thinking?
diapos.reponse: Not necessarily: Turing replaces a philosophical question with an observable test. Passing the test does not prove understanding.
diapos.explication: This is the objection raised by the philosopher John Searle (1980) with the Chinese room, which we will see in session 2.
diapos.notes: 10 min of discussion. Let both sides speak before showing the answer. Point to bring out: the test measures a behavior, the ability to pass for a human in writing; it does not define intelligence and does not prove understanding.

diapos.definition: The tendency to attribute intelligence, or even real understanding, to a program that talks.
diapos.exemple: In 1966, users of ELIZA, which merely rephrased their sentences with simple rules, believed it truly understood them.
diapos.notes: Link it to the game: if the class hesitated over Y, who applied only four rules, that is the ELIZA effect. It also applies to today’s chatbots: answering well does not prove understanding.

points: Reducing AI to robots or to recent chatbots
Believing that a system understands because it answers well: this is the **ELIZA effect**
Taking the Turing test for a **definition** of intelligence
diapos.notes: Reread these three mistakes and ask, for each one, what in the session helps to correct it. Expected: the definition through tasks and the family of techniques (1); the “machine’s” rule card (2); the fact that Turing proposes an observable test, not a definition (3).
